approach: Retrospective analysis of a prospective cohort of patients treated in Phase I trials at VHIO over the last 7 years. Two cohorts were identified: those receiving ICIs (n=310) and those receiving targeted agents (n=281). Patients who received chemotherapy within 4 months of their respective prior therapy were selected (n=31 for ICI group, n=52 for TA group). Outcomes measured were Response Rate (RR) based on RECIST criteria (PR, SD, PD) and Progression-Free Survival (PFS). Statistical analysis included univariate logistic regression for factors linked to RR and propensity score (PS) matching to compare median PFS between the two sequential treatment arms, adjusting for confounders such as number of previous lines and cancer type.

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Provides empirical evidence from a real-world prospective cohort regarding the sequence of ICI followed by chemotherapy in advanced solid tumors, testing the 'sensitization' hypothesis against a targeted agent control.
contribution_and_limits.limits: Small sample size in the matched analysis (31 vs 52 patients); observational design limits causal inference; single-center data (VHIO); lack of mechanistic data linking microbiome or immune status to outcomes; abstract does not detail the specific chemotherapy regimens used.

key_findings.finding: Numerically higher partial response rate (PR) with chemotherapy after ICIs (16.1%) compared to after TAs (7.7%), but the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.43). Stable disease rates were also higher after ICIs (16.4% vs 34.6% SD? Note: Abstract says SD 16.4% for ICI and 34.6% for TA, implying lower SD stability or different distribution, but PD was higher in ICI group 64.5% vs 57.7%). Factors associated with higher RR were fewer previous treatment lines (OR 0.51) and breast cancer histology (OR 5.54).

Median PFS for chemotherapy after ICIs was 2.3 months (95% CI 1.8-5.3) versus 3.2 months (95% CI 2.3-5.3) after TAs. The hazard ratio was 1.01 (95% CI 0.59-1.74; p = 0.96), indicating no significant difference in survival outcomes.

problem_or_question: To determine if anti-tumor activity of chemotherapy is enhanced ('sensitized') when given after immune checkpoint inhibitors compared to after targeted agents in patients with refractory advanced solid tumors.
research_scope: Refractory advanced solid tumors; prospective cohort from Phase I trials at Vall d'Hebron Institute Oncology (VHIO); comparison between post-ICI and post-targeted agent (TA) chemotherapy sequences.
work_summary: This study investigates whether prior exposure to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) sensitizes patients with refractory advanced solid tumors to subsequent chemotherapy (Ctx), a hypothesis suggested by preliminary data in Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma. Using a retrospective analysis of a prospective cohort, the authors compared the response rate (RR) and progression-free survival (PFS) of chemotherapy administered after ICIs versus chemotherapy administered after targeted agents (TAs). The analysis employed propensity score matching to adjust for clinical-pathological heterogeneity. The results showed no statistically significant difference in RR or PFS between the two groups, suggesting that, within this specific cohort and setting, ICIs do not provide a clear sensitization advantage over TAs for subsequent chemotherapy in solid tumors.
